newsitem.title: USA: U.S. to appeal Honduran refusal to extradite Francois.
newsitem.headline: U.S. to appeal Honduran refusal to extradite Francois.

text.p: U.S. authorities will appeal against a Honduran judge's decision to turn down their request for the extradition of former Haitian police colonel Joseph Michel Francois to face drug trafficking charges, a Justice Department spokesman said on Wednesday.
Judge Marco Alvarado said in Tegucigalpa the United States had three days to appeal or he would order Francois released.
"We are informing the judge we plan to appeal," said John Russell, a spokesman for the Justice Department in Washington.
Alavardo announced his decision denying the extradition on Wednesday morning.
"We disagree with the judge's ruling," Russell said. "We've been in touch with our embassy and asked our charge d'affaires to tell the judge."

Honduran police backed by U.S. agents arrested Joseph, the feared police chief of the Haitian capital Port-au-Prince during the 1991-1994 military government, on March 7 in San Pedro Sula. He was living there in exile after fleeing Haiti following the 1994 U.S. invasion that toppled the junta.

U.S. Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA) officials had planned to bring him directly to Miami and into court and were dismayed when Honduran legal authorities held up the operation as he was being escorted to the airport.

The U.S. indictment against Francois said he used his position as police chief to turn Haiti into a vast staging post to ship thousands of pounds of cocaine and heroin to the United States in league with Colombian drug barons.

Francois was believed to have been the mastermind behind the September 1991 coup that toppled President Jean-Bertrand Aristide. As the capital's police chief, he created a network of plainclothes policemen known as "attaches" who terrorised opponents of the regime.

Eduardo Gamarra, an expert on narcotics trafficking at Florida International University's Latin American and Caribbean Centre, said extradition was a touchy subject in Honduras because of a previous U.S. action over Honduran cocaine baron Ramon Mata Ballasteros.

U.S. agents kidnapped Mata Ballasteros in Honduras in 1988 and took him to the United States for trial, where he is now serving time in a maximum security prison. But that U.S. action infuriated Honduran public opinion.
Gamarra also noted that the U.S.-trained Francois was widely reputed to have been in the pay of U.S. intelligence agencies at times in his career.
"You have to wonder what other agencies are involved. U.S. agencies are not always on the same page," he said.

"It's a blow to the DEA but not that big a blow," Gamarra added. "It's more a symbolic thing. Francois was a big fish but he's no longer significant unless he's doing things in Honduras we don't know about, which is always possible."
Bill O'Neill of the National Coalition for Haitian Rights said he was disappointed by Judge Alvarado's decision.
"I think a U.S. court would be best equipped to uncover just what Francois did, not just in drug trafficking but in the persecution and terror in Haiti under the military regime."
It could also have helped to bring others to justice, he said from the coalition's New York office.
"Haitian courts and police are not capable of dealing with this. It's going to slow down the development of justice in Haiti," O'Neill said.
